readings.title: A large-print collection that circulates
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A library expanded its large-print shelves. Readers welcomed the investment but found most new titles concentrated in one genre. The main obstacle was a collection chosen without enough reader input. Purchase decisions relied on one supplier catalogue rather than local requests. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used borrowing patterns and confidential suggestions. Librarians compared circulation with themes requested by regular and new visitors. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated varied genres mattered more than a larger single shelf. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a rotating purchase list shaped by requests. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: access includes meaningful choice. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in a large-print collection that circulates, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Explaining an ebook loan
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A public library offered ebooks. Some borrowers downloaded a book successfully but could not understand why it disappeared after two weeks. The main obstacle was loan rules hidden in technical language. The app showed a small due date without explaining automatic return. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used a guided first-loan session. Staff asked volunteers to describe what they expected to happen at each screen. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated a short explanation prevented surprise. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced clear due-date messages before borrowing. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: digital services need familiar explanations. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in explaining an ebook loan, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Editing a community newsletter
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A neighbourhood newsletter invited short articles. Volunteers spent hours shortening submissions because the requested length was never stated. The main obstacle was contribution guidance without word limits. Writers sent pieces ranging from a few lines to several pages. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used a review of recent editing work. Editors noted which changes were routine and asked contributors what guidance would help. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated examples saved time for both sides. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a simple contributor guide with sample lengths. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: clear expectations support volunteer publishing. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in editing a community newsletter, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A book discussion across languages
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
An adult reading circle included people reading in different languages. A single English edition made some members reluctant to join. The main obstacle was discussion tied to one edition. Participants could share ideas about the story even when wording differed across translations. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used a trial meeting focused on themes and scenes. Facilitators asked readers to bring a passage in their preferred edition and explain its context. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated shared questions welcomed more readers. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced topic prompts that work across editions. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: reading communities can value different routes to a text. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in a book discussion across languages, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
Projects concerning reading, publishing and access to information often begin with a practical question. People may agree on a general goal while experiencing the same service in different ways. In this case, local organizers invited residents to describe ordinary visits and kept simple records of what happened. They compared those accounts before changing the community reading access programme. The first trial did not answer every question, but it showed which difficulties were repeated and which were temporary. Staff then explained the reasons for a modest adjustment. Clear information helped people understand the decision, including those who would have preferred another option. The group planned to review the arrangement again after more people had used it.
translation.explanation: 参考译文供考生自评，注意语义准确、逻辑关系及汉语通顺。
translation.referenceAnswer: 有关阅读出版与信息获取的项目通常从一个实际问题开始。人们可能赞同总体目标，却对同一服务有不同体验。在这个案例中，当地组织者请居民描述日常使用情况，并简单记录发生的事情。他们对照这些叙述后调整了服务。最初的试行无法回答所有问题，但能显示哪些困难反复出现，哪些只是暂时现象。工作人员随后解释了一项适度调整的原因。清楚的信息帮助人们理解决定，包括那些更希望采用其他方案的人。团队计划在更多人使用后再次评估安排。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the publishing and reading team proposing a small improvement to the community reading access programme. Explain the problem, describe a short trial, and say what evidence should guide the final decision.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the community reading access programme. People have noticed a collection chosen without enough reader input, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
